notes.text: They have got possession of the City of Zarahemla. The rebels, unmindful of anything except their own personal advantages, drove, as we have noted, the rightful administrative body of the government into asylum at Gideon. There Pahoran, the Chief Governor of the whole land, found inviolable sanctuary, and under the protection afforded by that retreat carried on a campaign of righteousness aimed at preserving the integrity of the Nephite Commonwealth. The effrontery, or shameless boldness, of the disaffected knew no bounds. They sought to turn the Republic into a kingdom, and went so far as to appoint a king over them. They selected an ambitious leader of the insurgent forces, a man named Pachus (Chapter 62:6) to be their king. Cruel, relentless, and hardhearted, he developed a plan of personal victory which in itself was a devilish conspiracy. He wrote to the King of the Lamanites seeking his help in its success. The bribe Pachus offered him was a downright surrender to the Nephite's traditional enemy. The king's acceptance of the terms of this evil

quotes.text: I, Pahoran, do not seek for power. Pahoran was not hasty to take umbrage at Moroni's criticism of his personal conduct. He knew that if half of what Moroni believed was true, then he had a justifiable cause for censure. However, Pahoran, the Chief Judge, a just man himself, prompt in his actions and thoughts, resolved in his own conscience-that court of righteous and holy decisions-that Moroni was blameless of evil intent, and that his hostile condemnation of Pahoran's seeming inaction was impelled by a desire to see that justice was done his men that they in turn, might successfully defend their homes, their liberty, their God and their religion, and their country. He assured Moroni that he was not angry because of the acrimony the words of Moroni evinced in writing to him, It mattereth not, Pahoran said, but I do rejoice in the greatness of your heart. I, Pahoran, do not seek for power, was the pledge he offered Moroni in explaining, if any were needed, of his integrity to the cause they both held dear; he was not interested in, or influenced by regard for his own welfare save only, he noted, to retain my Judgment-Seat that I may preserve the rights and the liberty of my people.

notes.text: 10-14 We will resist evil even unto bloodshed. Here, again, is manifested the spirit of the Gospel of Christ in Pahoran's words wherein he expresses forbearance for them that transgress God's Laws. But wickedness, itself, he informs us he will not endure. We will resist wickedness even unto bloodshed, was his counsel. And here again Pahoran offers no apologies or pretexts for his determination to stamp out rebellion against God and man even unto the death of those who carry on. As for the Lamanites, he said that we will not invade their lands, we seek only for peace, but, on the other hand, if they leave their own territory and violate ours, we will, in our defense, shed their blood. And our brethren, the Nephites who take up the sword against us who are rightfully installed in places of governmental responsibility and authority, we must suppress them even by bloodshed, and acclaim anew the liberty in the which God has made us free. If, Pahoran said, the Lord required that we submit ourselves to the yoke of bondage and give ourselves up to our enemies, we will gladly keep His commandments, in order to hasten the end He has in view for them. notes.text: 15-18 Therefore, come unto me speedily with a few of your men. Pahoran, after explaining to Moroni the sore strait of affairs into which the government of the Republic at Zarahemla had been plunged by the rebellion of Pachus and his men, and also after expressing to him the mutual confidence each had in the purposes of the Lord, called upon Moroni for military assistance in combatting the evil of a divided people-that is, of one being pitted against the other. Come unto my help with a few men, admonished the Chief Judge, and the remainder of your corps leave in charge of Lehi and Teancum that they, under the influence of the Holy Spirit, which is the Spirit of Freedom, may carry on the war in that part of the land. We may conceive that Pahoran sent his request to Moroni for aid not without a prayer to Him Whose servant he was, which prayer was not unlike the prayer offered by the Jews today: Almighty God, in all our trials we turn unto Thee, Who art our ever-present help in time of trouble. Forsake us not nor abandon us. Make us feel that Thou art near unto all who call upon Thee, who call upon Thee in truth. Guide us by Thy counsel and lead us in Thy love. And we imagine that he added the hallowed thought, May we find favor in Thy sight. (Union Prayer Book) Pahoran did not ask for help without giving his plans considerable thought. He had them already mapped out, probably inspired and in righteousness formulated. To stave off hunger and its resultant evils,

Together, they could regain possession of Zarahemla. From its well-stocked supplies they then would send Lehi and Teancum adequate food; Yea, Pahoran confidently noted to Moroni in speaking of the rebels, We will go forth against them in the strength of the Lord, and we will put an end to this great iniquity.
